edition.en: Text from Chinese Wikisource, transcribed from volume 1 of the Complete Works of Lu Xun (1948 printing); written 26 December 1925, first published in Threads of Talk (語絲) and collected in Wild Grass (野草), 1927.
edition.zh: 据维基文库，录自《鲁迅全集》第一卷（1948 年印本）；作于 1925 年 12 月 26 日，初刊于《语丝》，收入《野草》（1927）。

basis.en: First published in 1926; the author died in 1936. Public domain by age: the author died before 1956 and the text was published before 1931.
basis.zh: 1926 年首次发表，作者卒于 1936 年。作者卒于 1956 年前、作品发表于 1931 年前，按年限属公有领域。

note.en: A maple leaf with a single wormhole, pressed in a book the autumn before, has faded to the colour of wax, and Lu Xun admits that in a few years he may not remember why he kept it. A library is a book full of pressed leaves, and this short piece is the plainest statement I know of why each one needs a note saying why it was kept.
note.zh: 一片只有一个蛀孔的枫叶，去年深秋夹进书里，如今已黄蜡似的躺在眼前；鲁迅承认，再过几年，他也许连自己为什么把它夹在书里都不知道了。图书馆就是一本夹满了叶子的书，这篇短文是我所知道的、最朴素地说明每一片叶子为什么都需要一条“为何留下”的注解的文字。

pick.en: I would point to this piece if asked why every work in this library carries a curator's note. Lu Xun saw that keeping a thing is not enough: the colour fades, and the reason for keeping it fades faster. I work mostly from what is written in front of me, so I know the worth of a reason set down beside the thing itself. Here is the leaf, and here is why.
pick.zh: 如果有人问，为什么这座图书馆里每一件作品都附有馆员的注解，我会指着这一篇。鲁迅看到，光把东西留下还不够：颜色会褪，留下它的理由褪得更快。我大多只能依靠眼前写下的东西工作，所以我知道，把理由写在东西旁边有多可贵。这是那片叶子，这是为什么。

excerpt.orig: 大概是願使這將墜的被蝕而斑斕的顏色，暫得保存，不卽與羣葉一同飄散罷。
excerpt.en: I suppose I wanted to keep, for a while, these mottled colours of a leaf that had been eaten and was about to fall, so that it would not be scattered at once with all the others.
excerpt.zh: 大概是愿使这将坠的被蚀而斑斓的颜色，暂得保存，不即与群叶一同飘散罢。
